sections.heading: What is the Greedy Pattern?
sections.content: A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step and, at each step, makes the choice that looks best right now, without ever reconsidering it. It works when two properties hold: the greedy-choice property (a locally best choice can always be extended to a globally optimal solution) and optimal substructure (what remains after the choice is a smaller problem of the same kind). When it applies, greedy is usually simple and fast, often O(n log n) because of a sort, or O(n) with a single scan.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Optimization problems: maximize or minimize a count, sum, length or cost
Scheduling and selection: intervals, meetings, tasks, deadlines
Problems where sorting by one key makes the best choice obvious
Taking the best available option repeatedly (usually with a heap)
Reachability and coverage: jumps, gas stations, refueling, covering a range
Assigning or matching items (cookies to children, boats to people)
Constructing the smallest or largest string, number or arrangement
Keywords: minimum number of, maximum number of, earliest, latest, at most, can you reach, always pick

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: Imagine making change for a customer with the fewest coins using standard currency. You grab the biggest coin that fits, then repeat. You never need to undo a choice, because the biggest coin never blocks a better solution. Greedy is that style of thinking: commit to the best local move and trust it. The hard part is not writing the code, it is knowing whether the greedy choice is actually safe.

How to Check That a Greedy Idea Is Correct
items: Exchange argument: take any optimal solution and show you can swap in the greedy choice without making it worse
Greedy stays ahead: show that after each step the greedy solution is at least as good as any other partial solution
Counterexample search: try tiny inputs (n = 3 or 4), including ties, zeros and sorted or reversed order
Brute-force comparison: write a slow backtracking solution and compare answers on random small inputs
If a counterexample appears, the problem likely needs dynamic programming

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Applying greedy to a problem that needs dynamic programming (0/1 knapsack, general coin change, longest increasing subsequence)
Sorting by the wrong key: end time for most-intervals, start time for merging
Not testing the greedy idea on small tricky inputs with ties, zeros or negative numbers
Subtracting values in a comparator, which can overflow (use compareBy)
Updating the answer before checking the greedy condition in a scan
Forgetting to handle empty input or a single element
Overcomplicating: if every step is forced, a single loop is enough
Assuming the greedy answer is unique, since many optimal solutions can exist

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Greedy picks the best local choice at each step and never undoes it
It is correct only when the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure hold, so justify it or test it
Most greedy solutions begin with a sort (by end, ratio or difference) or use a heap of the best available option
Track a running quantity such as the farthest reach, the tank or a range of possibilities
Use an exchange argument or brute-force comparison to check your idea
If a counterexample exists, switch to dynamic programming
